candidates.title: The Room
candidates.reason: Christian Volckman's 2019 film makes the wish-granting room and its limits a continuing mystery, not just an opening gimmick. Matt investigates the house's old murders and concealed wiring; the couple learns that objects made by the room decay outside the property, that a wished-for child ages at an alarming rate outside, and that the former resident John Doe was himself a creation whose survival depends on a further rule. In the final act the room's capacity to make convincing copies and a nested house becomes a practical deception/escape problem. These are separate intermediate discoveries across the film, supporting unknown_rules and revelation_frequency independently of the strong initial central_mystery. Limits: the actual origin of the room is never established; after the child appears, family conflict and increasingly violent horror occupy substantial time, and critics identify implausible decisions and a messy third act. It is a contained, rule-discovery mystery with meaningful operational answers, not a fully explained scientific-origin puzzle.

candidates.title: The Tourist
candidates.reason: Across both completed six-episode seasons, the central problem is who the amnesiac man actually is, why pursuers want him dead, and how his past connects to seemingly unrelated people. TVMaze's complete episode guide shows continuing inquiries and discoveries rather than only a pilot hook: season one tracks a mystery caller, Luci, a pursuing detective, an old acquaintance and the final identification of his criminal past. Season two moves the inquiry to Ireland and changes the account again through the Cassidy/McDonnell feud, a missing diver, a concealed suitcase and family relationships; the finale resolves the immediate feud through letters and identifies a hidden killer, while a file supplies an additional secret-agent identity clue to the viewer. Netflix's full-season explanation and Den of Geek's finale breakdown substantiate the payoffs and reversals. This is a fast, suspenseful investigation/identity puzzle with regular discoveries, not a supernatural or time-anomaly show. Limits: season two devotes a substantial portion to criminal-family warfare and the central couple's trust, several twists are contrived, and the last agent revelation deliberately leaves a new backstory unresolved; investigation and twistiness should not be inflated into perfect progressive explanation.

research_rejections.title: The Nines
research_rejections.reason: The three-part construction builds recurring nines and identity/reality anomalies, but the second Hollywood-production chapter diverts much of the runtime away from solving the question. Whole-film critical assessments from Slant and Metacritic describe a largely climactic metaphysical explanation with a payoff some found unconvincing. This does not provide sufficient confidence in sustained revelation cadence and progressive reframing despite its appealing simulated-reality premise.

research_rejections.title: The Resort
research_rejections.reason: TVMaze and TV Guide episode guides confirm that the eight-episode missing-persons investigation does continue through the season and eventually finds Sam and Violet in Pasaje, so the premise is not abandoned. However, full-season reviews at Rotten Tomatoes, Metacritic and The Hollywood Reporter identify unsatisfied narrative questions, a mystical rather than clearly explained resolution, and an increasing emphasis on marriage, grief and time's emotional meaning. Insufficient confidence in explanatory payoff for Mystery's specific profile, despite its actual investigative activity.
